title: How do you calculate weighted averages quickly in a case interview?
description: Weighted averages explained with case examples: blended margins, average prices across segments, and how mix changes move the average.
hook: Multiply each value by its weight (usually its share of sales or volume), add the results, and divide by the total weight. Weighted averages appear in many cases without being named, as a blended margin across products or an average price across customer groups, and taking a simple average instead is one of the most common maths slips.
body:
The idea

An ordinary average treats every item equally. A weighted average gives each item a weight that reflects how much of it there is. If 90% of a company's sales are at a 10% margin and 10% are at a 50% margin, the company's margin is much closer to 10% than to 30%. A simple average ignores that.

The method

  1. Multiply each value by its weight.
  2. Add up the results.
  3. Divide by the total weight.
  4. Check that the answer sits between the lowest and highest values, closer to the one with more weight. If it does not, you have a unit or arithmetic error.

A worked example: blended margin

A company sells two products. Product A has $60M of sales at a 10% margin. Product B has $40M of sales at a 30% margin.

  • Wrong: (10% + 30%) ÷ 2 = 20%.
  • Right: ($60M × 10% + $40M × 30%) ÷ $100M = ($6M + $12M) ÷ $100M = 18%.

The answer is below 20% because the lower-margin product carries more weight.

A faster way with two groups

Start from the lower value and add the higher group's share of the gap: 10% + (40% × 20 points) = 10% + 8% = 18%. It is the same calculation, rearranged so you only need one multiplication.

Mix effects: the average moves even if nothing else does

Next year, sales shift to $80M of A and $20M of B. Neither product's margin changes and total sales stay at $100M. The blended margin becomes ($8M + $6M) ÷ $100M = 14%, and profit falls from $18M to $14M.

Nothing got worse within either product. The mix shifted towards the low-margin one. This is a mix effect, and it is often the hidden answer in a profitability case.

The same thing happens with prices. A subscription business has 100 premium customers paying $40 a month and 400 budget customers paying $10. Revenue is 100 × $40 + 400 × $10 = $8,000 across 500 customers, an average of $16 per customer (not the simple mean of $25). If the mix shifts to 250 of each, with no price change, revenue becomes $12,500 and the average rises to $25. The reported average improved without anyone raising a price.

Separating mix from rate

When both the mix and the segment values change, split the movement in two. Suppose in year two product A's margin also improves from 10% to 11%:

  • Year 1: 18.0% blended margin.
  • Year 2 at year 1 margins (mix only): 80% × 10% + 20% × 30% = 14.0%. Mix effect: −4.0 points.
  • Year 2 actual: 80% × 11% + 20% × 30% = 14.8%. Rate effect: +0.8 points.

Total change: −3.2 points, almost entirely from mix. That changes the recommendation: the fix is to win back sales of B, not to squeeze A's costs.

Strong: "Margin fell 3.2 points, but four points of that is mix: sales shifted to the lower-margin product. Within each product, margins actually held or improved. So the question is why B's sales fell."
Weak: "Margin fell from 18% to 14.8%, so we need to cut costs."

Common mistakes

  • Taking a simple average of rates or prices across groups of different sizes.
  • Using the wrong weights. Margins should be weighted by revenue, not units. Product A sells 1,000 units at $10 with a 50% margin; product B sells 100 units at $500 with a 10% margin. Weighted by revenue ($10k and $50k), the blended margin is ($5k + $5k) ÷ $60k = 16.7%. Weighting by units gives 46.4%, which is nonsense.
  • Weights that do not add up to 100%. Check before you multiply.

Practice

1. 70% of customers pay $10 and 30% pay $20. What is the average price?

Show the answer

0.7 × $10 + 0.3 × $20 = $7 + $6 = $13. Or with the shortcut: $10 + 30% × $10 = $13.

2. A hotel sells 60 room nights at $200 and 40 at $350. What is the average rate?

Show the answer

(60 × $200 + 40 × $350) ÷ 100 = ($12,000 + $14,000) ÷ 100 = $260. Shortcut: $200 + 40% × $150 = $260. It is below the simple average of $275 because more nights sold at the lower rate.
